newsitem.title: GERMANY: Court hits E.German leaders with arrest warrants.
newsitem.headline: Court hits E.German leaders with arrest warrants.

text.p: A Berlin court issued arrest warrants on Thursday against Egon Krenz, East Germany's last hardline communist leader, and three other former Politburo members to prevent them from leaving the country.
The court said a higher court ruling this week that East German leaders could be jailed for border killings had increased the chances Krenz and his former comrades would flee.

In a strongly worded statement, the Berlin court trying the former leaders for manslaughter said they would not have to go into custody but must give up their passports and face restrictions on their movements.
"The accused are under great suspicion of carrying out these crimes," the court's written judgment said. It also warned they could face stiff sentences if convicted.

Krenz and his co-defendants have been on trial for the past year, accused of responsibility for the deaths of East Germans killed trying to flee to the West over the Berlin Wall or across the fortified Cold War frontier between the two Germanys.
"Up until now they did not have to reckon with a serious sentence," the court said. "This situation changed with the decision by the Federal Constitutional Court."

The Constitutional Court, Germany's highest, ruled on Tuesday that East German leaders could be held legally responsible for border killings, removing an important line of defence for the former Politburo members.
Krenz, who ruled East Germany for three weeks in 1989 after longtime leader Erich Honecker quit, insisted he had no plans to leave Germany and would continue to take part in the trial.
"I will face this trial because I have nothing to hide," said Krenz, 59, who is on trial with former top officials Guenter Schabowski, Guenther Kleiber and Horst Dohlus.
The first effects of the Constitutional Court ruling were apparent on Wednesday, when former East German border guard chief Klaus-Dieter Baumgarten was arrested.
Baumgarten had already been convicted for his part in border killings but had not been jailed pending the ruling.
Krenz said the court decisions proved there was one law for west Germans and another for east Germans.
"We don't just have first and second-class citizens in Germany, we also have first and second-class law," he said.
But he remained defiant, saying outside the Berlin court: "I won't be brought to my knees -- not yesterday, not today, not tomorrow."

The extreme secrecy surrounding East Germany's fortified borders has made it impossible to know how many people were shot dead or killed by landmines as they tried to flee west from the 1950s to the fall of the Wall on November 9, 1989. Estimates range from 250 to 800.

Berlin courts have convicted 29 lower-ranking border guards of murder but given most of them suspended sentences because they were young recruits following orders. Honecker was let off on health grounds.

Six former East German generals in charge of border security were sentenced in September to prison terms of between three to six years for instructing guards on how to shoot and lay mines to stop refugees.
